items.title: Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning
items.content:
Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computer proof assistants like Lean can verify—can help.

Last month, Claude completed the first formalized proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, one of the most famous theorems of all time. This was a project experts thought would take many years. It is the largest Lean proof ever written.

Fermat’s Last Theorem was first proven in 1995 by Sir Andrew Wiles, more than 350 years after it was conjectured. Our proof, which totals over 13 million lines of code, provides machine verification. More importantly, it proves over 29,000 other theorems that the proof requires, across many areas of math which had never before been formalized.

We see this as a major step in the long process of firming up the core of mathematical knowledge, building on work from three centuries of mathematicians and hundreds of contributors to Lean and Mathlib. We are optimistic that AI-assisted verification of mathematical proofs will help reduce the burden of refereeing mathematics in an era where more proofs are being produced than ever before.

You can read about the process on our Science Blog: https://t.co/ryYnDEAU6J

And see the complete proof on GitHub: https://t.co/wlYMXYnofz

items.title: I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and ge
items.content:
I spent much of the weekend talking with the team who did this work. Seb--and everyone else--acted with integrity and generosity throughout.

Initially we believed the other team had also solved the problem. We wanted to collaborate and do a joint release. 

When we learned that they had Euler but not Navier-Stokes, we offered to let them go first, to suggest that they should be the ones to get the prize, and optionally for Tristan to be the lead author on a rewrite of the OpenAI proof. We felt it was challenging to offer the same to Levent (an Anthropic employee), who was not willing to talk or coordinate with us anyway. We were open to other solutions.

We would have greatly preferred coordination. We did not rush to publish even though the other team wasn't communicating with us. The team threatened us with unfounded accusations of plagarism.

Now that we can see their work, the approaches appear to be different. It is also worth noting that our latest model can solve many, many other math problems.

It is true that we tried this because there were rumors on the internet last week that Anthropic's models had solved a millennium problem and we were curious if ours could do it too.

items.content:
The economic model breaks jobs down into bundles of tasks. AI can help someone complete a task faster or better, do the task itself, leave the task untouched, or create new tasks. 

Based on how you expect AI to affect tasks by 2030, our scenario explorer models AI’s potential impact on the US economy.

The scenario explorer focuses on three possible scenarios: modest, substantial, and extreme. The economy grows across all three scenarios. But in more transformative scenarios, AI automates more knowledge work, so the challenge is making sure that the gains are shared across society.

Like all economic models, ours simplifies a more complex reality. But by building better scenarios of our possible economic future, we can take steps to make sure everyone benefits from it.

I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more
items.content:
I showered with my AI, and it was a horrible mistake.

As the world gets more AI-friendly, and as we find more and more things to be productive about (and I don't want everything in my life to actually be productive), I have been testing and experimenting with AI usage in different contexts.

And Codex live voice mode opened up new options for me.

One time, instead of waiting to clean my apartment at the end of the day or on the weekend, I actually did it during the workday while I was dictating to Codex and processing tasks that I had to do.

Another time, I had to fill out this form for my Apple Business account. And Codex did it all for me - it even found my W-9 on my laptop to pull my EIN. It completed the whole form so that I could run errands.

Instead of being strapped to my computer and having to dig up all these files and numbers on my own, I could do double duty and get personal things off my plate without losing time.

I use AI on walks. And importantly, it's not that I'm adding AI to the walks that I'm already doing (for that, I still prefer Sam Cooke or Hello Puzzlers). It's that I'm able to TAKE MORE WALKS that I wasn't able to before because of AI.

So now, I might go on a walk at 4pm and process all the Slack messages that I didn't respond to or review a client contract. As a team, sometimes we even take team-wide walk breaks to work 1:1 with our AIs.

BUT. 

I just tried one new workflow that I hated with the fury of a thousand suns.

And that was trying voice mode while I was in the shower.

It was effective in the sense that the AI could hear me well and could process tasks (unlike the Apple AI assistant who shall remain nameless, who can't hear me if a single pin is dropped in the background).

Sure, there was a little annoyance when the phone had a permission pop-up and I had to reach my hand out of the shower to press it.

But my biggest gripe was that I just hated the overall experience. Hated it. 

There are some parts of my life that I really don't want to add AI into right now.

And it's really in those times where I allow my brain to dance off into the edges of my imagination, or truly relax and take time away from execution.

And I just want this to be a reminder that we need space to be away from tech and just think and exist.

That could be on a nature hike, or in the shower, or my favorite meditative place in the whole wide world (the middle of a car wash).

There is no perfect optimization formula that is telling us that every minute of every day has to be AI-enabled.

So I will no longer be showering with my AI and will stick to my rubber duck.

Thank you.

Everyone wants to know whether their agent scores an 8 out of 10.

That is the wrong number to watch.

The score alone t
items.content:
Everyone wants to know whether their agent scores an 8 out of 10.

That is the wrong number to watch.

The score alone tells you little. Quality is subjective and it moves with the task. 70% similarity is fine for a marketing draft and unacceptable in a regulated process. There is no universal bar.

What matters is the deviation.

Your system holds steady around a seven. You ship a change. It drops to a five.

Something happened. That is the signal. The deviation matters more than the number itself.

Which makes evals more practical than teams expect. You do not need everyone to agree what a ten means. You need a consistent measure and a baseline you trust.

And you are almost never automating from thin air. There is an existing process, so examples of good already exist in your business. That is your test suite.

After that it is regression testing. New model, new prompt, check the outputs still land where they used to.

So what should you watch?

The drift.

items.title:
This is the AWS moment for agents.

OpenAI just shipped the Agents API, and everything that made agents hard to build is
items.content:
This is the AWS moment for agents.

OpenAI just shipped the Agents API, and everything that made agents hard to build is now something you rent instead of build. Keeping one running for days, remembering what it's doing, using tools, recovering when a step fails. Now it's an API call.

Before AWS, you had to buy and run your own servers, so only well funded teams could build real/scalable products.

AWS made the hard part rentable, and all the value moved up to whoever had the best idea for what to build on top. Same thing is happening here.

I'll be honest, my first reaction was that this is bad news for a lot of people I know. If your whole company is an agent platform, the thing you spent the last year building is now included for the price of tokens.

But the more I sat with it, the more I think it's really good news if you're building for one specific industry. Basically, vertical software type stuff.

If the hardest engineering just became a line item, then the only thing left that's actually hard is knowing the job. Like what counts as a done claim, what makes a filing get rejected, where the money leaks.

So the wedge now is owning one painful workflow with your own tools, data, approvals, and a clear ROI. Freight exceptions, insurance reviews, security triage, revenue leakage, healthcare admin, compliance ops.

I see a lot of doomers on X saying software is over (and sometimes I feel the same way), you'll just use Claude or ChatGPT for everything. 

BUT, if that were true, OpenAI wouldn't be shipping infrastructure for other people to build agents on.

They're telling you exactly what they think: the general model is theirs, the 10,000+ specific jobs it needs to be pointed at are yours.

I think software is just evolving. 

It's becoming an agent internet, and every layer of it, the tools, the workflows, the boring jobs, gets rebuilt for a user that doesn't have eyes or hands. 

That's a lot of companies waiting to be built.

Sonnet 5 for everyday. Haiku 4.5 for quick answers.

Now look right next to it. Effort. Set it to High.
Effort is how hard Claude thinks before answering. Almost nobody knows the dial is there.

→ Switch 2: Skill that works like prompt shortcuts

A skill is a long prompt turned into a command that runs on its own, every time.

Install /skill-creator first by Anthropic.
Then talk to it: "I need a skill that turns my messy notes into a client email in my voice."

It asks questions. You answer. It saves.
For my personal favourite Claude Skills.
Go to https://t.co/6cHYYfjXEA.
Download the skills.
Put your email and verify with an OTP.
Save the downloaded zip file.
Upload to Claude → Settings → Skills.

/anti-ai → rewrites until the detector calls it human. Built after $34 of breaking AI detectors.
/how-to → walks you A to Z through any task inside Claude. I built it to replace myself.
/fable-5 → your messy brain dump in, a Fable-optimised prompt out.
/hands-off → compresses a whole chat into a clean doc, so a new chat resumes with nothing lost.

Building your own takes weeks. So I handed mine over at https://t.co/6cHYYfjXEA 

→ Switch 4: four connectors. Not 40.

Claude Settings → Connectors.

✦ Granola → meeting transcript, inside Claude. Don't ask for the summary. Ask "what did I commit to in the last five calls, and what's still open."
✦ Gmail + Slack → turn both on together. One is what was promised in writing. The other is what was actually said in the thread.
✦ Google Drive → one button turns Claude's output into a real Sheet or Doc. No downloads folder.
✦ Gamma → a prompt to finished (with taste) slides.

Whatever you can open at work, Claude can open. Whatever you can't, it can't.

→ Switch 5: the one app that isn't inside Claude

Wispr Flow .ai (free). You speak your prompt instead of typing it. Nobody types 3 paragraphs of context. Everybody says three paragraphs out loud.

You speak 4x faster than you type.

→ Switch 6: skip this one if you're new

Role Plugins. Sales, Marketing, Finance, Ops.
Each is a ready-made bundle of skills. Useful once you know what you want. Confusing before that.

I've rebuilt this setup twice. Both times in 7 mins.

How to actually get into humanoid robotics in 2026, and this is where the money actually is right now.

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

start with ros 2. this is still the industry standard for communication, sensing, and control across nearly every real platform. don't jump straight to a humanoid, start on gazebo or webots, both free, both built for ros 2, both with strong documentation for a genuine beginner.

move into simulation before you touch real hardware. pybullet and mujoco for reinforcement learning specifically, mujoco is the actual physics engine behind a huge share of current humanoid locomotion research, deepmind and most academic labs run on it. isaac sim from nvidia if you want gpu-accelerated, photorealistic perception work, free to download, and nvidia's own "introduction to robotic simulations" self-paced course walks you through the exact ros 2 reference architecture.

learn vla models next, and treat this as mandatory, not optional. vision-language-action models are the actual shift that changed what's possible in the last two years, robots now take a spoken instruction, plan the motion sequence, and execute it, without task-specific programming. if you're in robotics and haven't studied vla architecture yet, you're already behind where the field currently sits.

hardware is more accessible than people assume. the so-101 robot arm, an open source platform, costs roughly $110 to build and has a genuinely active github ecosystem, teleoperation, imitation learning, and rl training all documented and reproducible. this is the actual entry point most self-taught people are using right now, not a $20,000 humanoid.

understand the two training methods actually being used at the frontier. imitation learning, where a robot watches human demonstration data (motion capture or teleoperation) and distills it into a policy. reinforcement learning, where the robot discovers a strategy through trial and error in simulation, tesla uses this specifically for balance, gait, and grip force problems that are too hard to demonstrate perfectly by hand. tesla's own "digital dreams" approach takes one real demonstration and generates 10,000 synthetic variations with realistic physics, solving the actual bottleneck in this field, you cannot physically demonstrate every scenario at the scale training requires.

the honest state of the industry right now. figure 02 already completed a 20-hour continuous shift. tesla optimus runs a full 8-hour workday on its current battery. boston dynamics' electric atlas is live in hyundai plants. this moved from research demo to real deployment in the last year, and the field is hiring specifically for the ros 2 plus vla skill combination right now.

items.content:
Show HN: MultiMatte, a Promptable Image Background Removal Model Hey HN, I'm Shreyash from Feyn. We help companies build custom models from their data.

Today we're releasing MultiMatte, a background removal model you can aim with words. Name an object in your image. MultiMatte keeps just that thing, and removes everything else.

Try it out on your images: https://usefeyn.com/multimatte/.

Demo video: https://youtu.be/XZ5BJWAkOjs

MultiMatte is open source. Build with it using our NoBg library https://github.com/feyninc/nobg. Model card here: https://hf.co/feyninc/multimatte

MultiMatte is the second iteration of our background removal models. The first was FeyNoBg, which we released here https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49072462.

The big upgrade is promptability. Most models keep all foreground elements when cutting the background. MultiMatte lets you prompt the exact objects you want to keep and remove everything else. For example, If you have an image with a dog and a bowl, you can ask MultiMatte to keep just the dog.

MultiMatte is built on Meta's SAM 3, a concept-promptable detector that already understands phrases. Our biggest change was in masking. Instead of binary masks that classify each pixel as being inside or outside an object, MultiMatte uses alpha mattes that assign an opacity value to each pixel, with respect to an object. This allows us to better represent hair, fur, motion blur, and other kinds of fuzzy boundaries.

Across all our measured benchmarks, MultiMatte shows a step improvement over SAM 3. On DIS5K, S-measure rises from 0.674 to 0.908 (a 34.6% relative gain), and on DUT-OMRON from 0.792 to 0.901 (13.7%).

Our blog covers more of the training details and results https://usefeyn.com/blog/multimatte.

Happy to answer any questions!

- 32 GB: larger local workflows.

LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI SDK, Google SDK. Which one should you use?  

The answer depends on how much of the agent’s
items.content:
LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI SDK, Google SDK. Which one should you use?  

The answer depends on how much of the agent’s control flow you need to own.

Use the OpenAI SDK or Google GenAI SDK when the problem is simple: call a model, pass structured input, use a few tools, and return a result. You get a direct provider interface with less abstraction and fewer moving parts. That makes it a good place to prototype and a good choice for provider-specific features.

But a direct SDK does not automatically give you a production agent.  

You still need iteration limits, retry budgets, persisted state, idempotency, tool permissions, per-step traces, timeouts, and a verified done check.

LangChain is useful when you want reusable building blocks: model adapters, prompts, tool wrappers, retrievers, loaders, structured output, and common agent components. It can help you move quickly, especially when you are experim

The trade-off is abstraction. A framework may hide how state is passed, how retries happen, how tool results are parsed, or where a failure actually occurred. That is fine until the trace shows you need more control.

LangGraph is for a different problem.

It gives you an explicit graph of nodes, edges, state transitions, branches, cycles, checkpoints, and interrupts. It is useful when the workflow needs human approval, durable execution, recovery after failure, conditional routing, or multiple steps that must coordinate without becoming one long prompt.

LangGraph is not simply LangChain 2.0, and it is not automatically a replacement for LangChain. You can use LangChain components inside a LangGraph workflow, or use LangGraph without adopting every LangChain abstraction.

Other options can make sense too. A lightweight custom orchestration layer may be better when your workflow is small and your team wants complete visibility. Temporal or similar workflow systems may be better when durable execution and operational guarantees matter more than LLM-specific abstractions. Provider-neutral gateways can help with routing and model switching, but they do not remove the need for a harness.

My rule:  

- Direct SDK for simple calls and provider-specific features. 
- LangChain for fast composition and prototyping. 
- LangGraph for explicit stateful agent workflows. 
- Custom code when the abstraction hides more than it helps. 
- Durable workflow infrastructure when failure recovery is a first-class requirement.

Start with the smallest layer that solves the problem.  

Add abstraction when it saves work.  

Remove abstraction when it hides a failure you need to see.  

The tool does not make the agent reliable. The execution design does.
